title: AstraDynamics POC scoping - latency SLOs
summary: POC scoping call to define latency/throughput SLOs for AstraDynamics conversational assistant POC. Discussed TTFT vs TPOT, target p95/p99 numbers, workload sizing, benchmark plan, measurement methodology, and timelines. Agreed on initial test matrix (small/med/large prompts, 90/99 percentile targets), sample QPS for pilot, and next steps to share benchmark scripts, security docs, and schedule infra access for tests.
topics: TTFT vs TPOT definitions and tradeoffs
p95 / p99 latency targets and acceptable ranges
Workload sizing: QPS, concurrency, prompt length distributions
Benchmark plan: synthetic vs production traces, test matrix
Measurement plan: warmup, KV cache, batching, metrics to collect
Deployment mode: hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC)
Timeline and success criteria for POC
transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-11-15 16:00 PST | Duration 45m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (AstraDynamics - Head ML Infra), Marcus Chen (CTO), Priya Iyer (SRE), Samir Patel (ML Eng), Emily Zhou (Product)

Summary (auto): Quick alignment on latency SLO framing — TTFT (time to first token) vs TPOT (time per output token), target p95/p99, plus agreement on a benchmark plan and rough timeline for the POC.

[00:00] Jordan Park: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we'll run 45 minutes, try to cover goals then go to the test plan. handoff to maya for the tech framing.
[00:22] Maya Singh: yeah hi all, quick context — redwood is proposing a pilot to validate latency SLOs for your assistant. i'll cover definitions first, then the recommended test matrix. note: i'll refer to TTFT and TPOT, sometimes folks call TPOT per-token latency.
[00:40] Lena Ortiz: quick one, TTFT for us matters because the UI shows spinner until first token. so even if throughput is fine, the UX feels bad if TTFT > ~300 ms.
[00:53] Maya Singh: totally, that's a common constraint. so for clarity: TTFT (time to first token) is the end-to-end latency from request arrival to first token emitted; TPOT (time per output token) is the steady-state per-token latency after streaming begins. both matter — TTFT for perceived responsiveness, TPOT for long outputs and throughput math.
[01:18] Samir Patel: and p95/p99 targets? we usually measure p95 and p99 for both metrics, yep?
[01:26] Maya Singh: yes p95 and p99 are standard. for the POC we suggested baseline targets: TTFT p95 <= 300 ms, p99 <= 650 ms for short prompts (<= 64 tokens); TPOT p95 <= 40-60 ms on our recommended dedicated setup for med outputs. but we can shift depending on model/quantization. these are starting numbers.
[01:48] Marcus Chen: that's fine as a starting point. our production goal is p95 TTFT <= 250 ms though — is that realistic?
[01:55] Maya Singh: it's aggressive but achievable with caching, kept KV cache warm, and dedicated low-latency instances. we should run a test matrix to see where the tradeoffs land.
[02:10] Jordan Park: quick calibration — we will test both hosted and dedicated variants in the POC. hosted is quickest to start, dedicated gives the lowest tail latencies. also we'll show quantized model variants.

--- Benchmark / Test matrix ---
[02:30] Maya Singh: proposed matrix:
- input classes: short (<=32 tokens), medium (32-128), long (128-512)
- models: baseline open model v1, quantized int8 variant, smaller distilled variant
- deployment modes: hosted (shared), dedicated (reserved GPUs), private VPC if you need network isolation
- scenarios: cold start (no KV cache), warm start (KV cache hit), steady-state streaming at 1, 5, 10 QPS
- percentiles: measure p50/p90/p95/p99 for TTFT and TPOT, plus throughput (tokens/sec) and CPU/GPU utilization

[03:25] Priya Iyer: i want to call out network contribution — our users are in EU and US, but the POC should run in your eu-west region to align. also we need to capture network RTT separately so we can isolate infra latency vs network.
[03:44] Maya Singh: good point — we'll run tests in eu-west and us-west and capture client->edge rtt as a separate metric. we'll also provide a tracer that records timestamps inside the runtime.

[03:58] Samir Patel: about measuring TTFT vs TPOT — do you recommend instrumenting in the client side or relying on your runtime logs?
[04:07] Maya Singh: both. client-side timestamps capture end-to-end and network effects; runtime-side (server) timestamps let you see internal queueing and kernel time. we'll provide a small harness that emits both.

[04:20] Emily Zhou: what's our expected QPS for the pilot? we want to simulate realistic spikes.
[04:26] Jordan Park: from your telemetry you mentioned 200k monthly active users and about 5k concurrent sessions at peak; for the POC let's simulate 5, 25, and 50 concurrent users which translates to ~1/5/10 QPS per model variant depending on interaction patterns. recommended synthetic loads: 1 QPS (low), 5 QPS (medium), 10 QPS (high) sustained for 10 minutes each with 5-minute warmups.

[04:58] Lena Ortiz: our conversation lengths are often 40-80 tokens per reply, occasionally longer. so med bucket is realistic.

--- Success criteria and SLOs ---
[05:10] Maya Singh: success criteria we propose:
- TTFT p95 <= 300 ms, TTFT p99 <= 650 ms for short prompts in dedicated; hosted may be slightly higher
- TPOT p95 <= 60 ms for typical models at targeted batch sizes
- Throughput: achieve target tokens/sec to support 10 QPS with <80% GPU utilization on dedicated nodes
- Quality: model output parity within expected bounds (we'll run a small eval set to ensure quantization doesn't regress)
- Operational: end-to-end observability (traces, per-route dashboards) and reproducible benchmark scripts

[05:55] Marcus Chen: what's acceptable for hosted tail latency? our budget might prefer hosted if it's close.
[06:02] Maya Singh: hosted p95 might be within 350-450 ms for TTFT depending on contention; p99 can spike higher but we'll test with rate limits and routing to minimize tails. we also demonstrate fallbacks to smaller models for overload.

[06:18] Priya Iyer: security check — we need SOC2, SSO (SAML), audit logs, KMS integration. will you provide security docs before infra access?
[06:27] Jordan Park: yes we'll send the security pack (SOC2 report, KMS options, SSO docs) as a follow-up.

--- Measurement details ---
[06:40] Maya Singh: measurement plan specifics:
1) Warmup: run 5 minutes of background requests to populate KV cache and JIT paths
2) Baselines: measure cold start single request latency (TTFT) for 10 runs to capture extremes
3) Steady state: run sustained load for 10 minutes at each QPS point; capture p50/90/95/99 for TTFT and TPOT
4) Sampling: collect per-request metadata (prompt length, model variant, batch size, cache hit/miss)
5) Isolation: collect network RTT and server-side timestamps to split network vs compute time
6) Repeat each test 3 times across different times to capture variability

[07:45] Samir Patel: do you support continuous batching and how will that affect TPOT?
[07:51] Maya Singh: yes runtime supports continuous batching and dynamic batching windows. TPOT will be lower with larger batch sizes but TTFT may suffer slightly due to waiting for batch window. we'll include tests with min-batch=1 and with batching enabled (batch sizes 4, 8, 16) to show tradeoffs.

[08:15] Lena Ortiz: what observability will we get? per-route latency, token counts, kernel metrics?
[08:22] Maya Singh: you get per-route and per-model dashboards, token-level cost breakdowns, GPU util, queue lengths, and tracing hooks. we can expose traces to your existing tracing backend or provide raw logs.

--- Timeline and responsibilities ---
[08:40] Jordan Park: proposed timeline:
- Day 0-3: legal/Security docs exchange and infra access (VPN/VPC creds)
- Day 3-7: deploy test harness and smoke tests in eu-west dedicated test env (or hosted equivalent)
- Day 8-14: run full benchmark matrix and collect data
- Day 15-18: analysis, tuning (batching/quantization), and presentation of results
- Week 3: decision point for expansion or production rollout

[09:10] Marcus Chen: sounds reasonable. do you need a sample of our production prompts?
[09:15] Maya Singh: yes please — a de-identified trace of 1k typical requests (prompt lengths, timestamps) helps shape the distribution. ideally CSV or ndjson.
[09:25] Lena Ortiz: security — we will share only de-identified data and will require an NDA addendum if needed.

[09:33] Jordan Park: noted. next steps we'll capture in the recap.

--- Risks / Open questions ---
[09:40] Maya Singh: open items:
- exact model variant you'll want us to test (we suggested ModelX-open-1 and q8 variant)
- whether POC runs on your VPC (private) vs Redwood dedicated hardware
- any special latency budget for EU users vs US

[09:58] Priya Iyer: can you provide the harness repo and example scripts? we'll run them from our infra too.
[10:03] Jordan Park: yes repo link will be shared; we'll include both client harness and server-side instrumentation.

--- Final recap and explicit next steps ---
[10:15] Jordan Park: recap: 1) we align on TTFT/TPOT framing and p95/p99 targets; 2) we'll share security docs, benchmark scripts, and model recommendation; 3) AstraDynamics to share de-identified traces and confirm region; 4) schedule infra access for day 3.
[10:35] Lena Ortiz: confirmed, we'll get the trace and start the internal approvals for infra access.
[10:42] Marcus Chen: thanks, excited to see the numbers.
[10:45] Jordan Park: great, we'll follow up with timeline and the security pack. thanks all.

Note: transcription contains minor speaker mislabels and occasional stutters; timestamps approximate.
